title: Transcript of Chair Powell's Press Conference -- September 17, 2025
summary: The Federal Reserve cut its policy interest rate by 25 basis points to a target range of 4% to 4¼% on September 17, 2025, citing a shift in the balance of risks toward downside employment risks and still-elevated inflation. Chair Powell emphasized that the FOMC is balancing dual-mandate goals amid a softer labor market (unemployment at 4.3%, payrolls at 29,000/month) and persistent inflation (PCE at 2.7%, core PCE at 2.9%). The median SEP projection shows the federal funds rate declining to 3.6% by end-2025 and 3.4% by end-2026.
key_points: Fed lowered target range for federal funds rate by ¼ percentage point to 4 to 4¼ percent
Unemployment rate rose to 4.3% in August; payroll job gains slowed to just 29,000 per month over the past three months
Total PCE inflation was 2.7% and core PCE inflation was 2.9% over the 12 months ending in August
Median SEP projection for federal funds rate: 3.6% at end of 2025, 3.4% at end of 2026, 3.1% at end of 2027
Chair Powell stated near-term inflation risks are tilted upward and employment risks tilted downward, requiring balance of dual mandate
Tariff effects on goods prices are being observed but their overall effects on activity and inflation remain uncertain
why_it_matters: This press conference provides the official rationale for the Fed's rate-cut decision and signals the policy path ahead. The balance of risks has shifted toward employment concerns while inflation remains above target, creating a delicate situation where the Fed is navigating between supporting a softening labor market and preventing inflation from becoming entrenched.
macro_context: The Fed is navigating a challenging environment where employment risks have risen (unemployment at 4.3%, weak payrolls) while inflation remains above target at 2.7-2.9% PCE. GDP growth has moderated to 1.5% in H1 2025 from 2.5% last year. The FOMC is communicating that policy is being adjusted toward a more neutral stance, with rate projections declining over the next two years. Tariff-related price pressures are being monitored but their persistence remains uncertain.
